q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

items.p: The town of Brenford once sent its fallen leaves to a landfill each autumn. In 2015, the town began collecting leaves separately and turning them into compost, which it now gives away to residents for their gardens. The program has cut the town's landfill fees and become one of its most popular services.
c: Brenford's leaf composting program saves money and is popular with residents.
Landfills charge high fees for accepting leaves.
Residents of Brenford prefer vegetable gardens to flower gardens.
Brenford stopped collecting leaves in 2015.
w: Landfill fees are a supporting detail, not the main idea.
The text never compares types of gardens.
Brenford changed how it handles leaves; it did not stop collecting them.
items.e: The text describes Brenford's switch to composting leaves and its two results: lower landfill fees and a popular free service.

items.q: According to the text, what does Reyna do during his morning practice?
items.p: Pianist Tomas Reyna practices for four hours every morning, but he rarely plays complete pieces during that time. Instead, he repeats short passages slowly, sometimes a single measure dozens of times, until each movement of his hands feels automatic. Only in the evening does he play full works from start to finish.
c: He repeats short passages slowly many times.
He plays complete works from start to finish.
He teaches students for four hours.
He listens to recordings of other pianists.
w: The text says he does this in the evening, not the morning.
Teaching is never mentioned.
Listening to recordings is never mentioned.
items.e: The text states that in the morning he "repeats short passages slowly," sometimes a single measure dozens of times.

items.p: Researchers studying a shrub that grows in a foggy coastal desert found that its leaves are covered in tiny grooves. Fog droplets collect in the grooves and run down to the base of the plant, where the roots absorb them. The shrub can survive for months without rain by relying on fog alone.
c: The shrub survives long periods without rain by channeling fog water to its roots.
Fog is common in every desert.
The shrub's roots grow deeper than those of other desert plants.
Researchers have not yet explained how the shrub survives.
w: The text describes one foggy desert, not all deserts.
Root depth is never compared.
The text explains exactly how the shrub survives.
items.e: The text explains the shrub's grooved leaves, how they move fog water to the roots, and that this lets it survive without rain.

items.q: According to the text, why do the librarians plan to redesign two study areas?
items.p: When the Halverson Library reopened after a renovation, its staff noticed that the new reading room, with its large windows and movable chairs, was full every afternoon. The old room, which had fixed desks and little daylight, had often sat empty. Librarians now plan to redesign two smaller study areas in the same style.
c: The new reading room's design proved popular with visitors.
The study areas were damaged during the renovation.
Visitors complained that the new reading room was too bright.
The old reading room had too many chairs.
w: The text mentions no damage.
The text reports that the bright room was full, not that people complained.
The old room's problem was fixed desks and little light, not too many chairs.
items.e: The new room was full every afternoon, so the librarians plan to copy its style in two study areas.

items.p: Before refrigerators were common, some households kept food cool in a zeer, a pair of clay pots with one set inside the other and wet sand packed between them. As water in the sand evaporates through the outer pot, it draws heat away from the inner pot. The simple device can keep vegetables fresh for days in hot, dry climates.
c: A zeer uses evaporation to keep food cool without electricity.
Clay pots are the best containers for storing sand.
Refrigerators were invented to replace zeers.
Vegetables spoil faster in dry climates than in humid ones.
w: The pots hold sand only as part of the cooling method.
The text does not explain why refrigerators were invented.
The text does not compare spoilage across climates.
items.e: The text describes what a zeer is, how evaporation cools it, and what it can do.

items.p: For decades, historians assumed that medieval farmers in the region rarely traveled more than a few miles from home. But account books recently found in a village archive record farmers selling wool at markets more than eighty miles away, sometimes several times a year. These records suggest that rural life was far less isolated than once believed.
c: Newly found records suggest that medieval farmers in the region traveled much more than historians had assumed.
Medieval farmers earned most of their income from selling wool.
Village archives are the most reliable source of medieval history.
Historians have long known that farmers traveled to distant markets.
w: The records show wool sales but not the share of farmers' income.
The text does not rank sources by reliability.
The text says historians assumed the opposite.
items.e: The text contrasts an old assumption with new evidence and concludes that rural life was less isolated than believed.

items.p: Architect Sun-Hee Park designs schools without long hallways. In her buildings, classrooms open onto shared central spaces where students from different grades gather between lessons. Park argues that hallways isolate students, while shared spaces encourage the informal conversations through which younger students learn from older ones.
c: Park designs schools around shared spaces because she believes they help students learn from one another.
Park believes classrooms should be larger than they usually are.
Hallways are the most expensive part of a school to build.
Students in Park's schools spend less time in classrooms.
w: Classroom size is never discussed.
Cost is never mentioned.
The text does not say how much time students spend in classrooms.
items.e: The text describes Park's hallway-free design and her reason for it: shared spaces encourage students to learn from each other.

items.q: According to the text, what did Ortiz find about towns whose downtown shops survived?
items.p: Economist Rafael Ortiz studied why some small towns kept their downtown shops while others lost them. He found that towns whose shops survived usually had a single organization, often run by the shop owners themselves, that planned shared events and advertised the downtown as a whole rather than store by store.
c: They usually had one organization that promoted the downtown as a whole.
They had more shops than other towns.
Their shop owners advertised only their own stores.
They had larger populations than other towns.
w: The number of shops is not discussed.
This is the opposite of what Ortiz found.
Population is never mentioned.
items.e: Ortiz found a shared organization that "advertised the downtown as a whole rather than store by store."

items.p: Octopuses are known for changing color, but biologist Mara Ilic was surprised to find that one species also changes the texture of its skin. When resting among rocks, these octopuses raise tiny bumps that mimic the surface of nearby stones, making them nearly impossible to spot even when their color does not match perfectly.
c: One octopus species camouflages itself by changing the texture of its skin as well as its color.
Octopuses cannot change color while they are resting.
Ilic discovered that octopuses can change color.
Octopuses prefer rocky areas because they are easy to see there.
w: The text never says resting octopuses cannot change color.
The text presents color change as already well known.
The octopuses use rocks to hide, not to be seen.
items.e: The text's focus is Ilic's finding that the species also changes skin texture to blend in with rocks.

items.q: According to the text, why does Adeyemi type her handwritten drafts herself?
items.p: Novelist Grace Adeyemi drafts her books by hand in notebooks, then types them herself, revising heavily as she goes. She says that typing a handwritten page forces her to reconsider every sentence, because she cannot simply copy text; she must decide again whether each line deserves to stay.
c: Typing her drafts makes her reconsider each sentence.
She dislikes the handwriting of her assistants.
Typing is faster than writing by hand.
Her publisher requires typed manuscripts.
w: Assistants are never mentioned.
Speed is not her reason.
Publisher requirements are never mentioned.
items.e: Adeyemi says typing "forces her to reconsider every sentence."

items.p: Elena had walked past the bakery every morning for a year without going in. Today, the smell of cinnamon stopped her at the door. She stood there long enough for the baker to look up and wave, and she found, to her own surprise, that she was already reaching for the handle.
c: Elena unexpectedly decides to enter a bakery she has passed many times.
Elena dislikes the smell of cinnamon.
The baker asks Elena to work at the bakery.
Elena visits the bakery every morning.
w: The smell draws her in, so she does not dislike it.
The baker only waves.
She passes the bakery every morning but has never gone in.
items.e: After a year of walking past, Elena is surprised to find herself reaching for the bakery's door.

items.p: When a small software company tried a four-day workweek, its managers expected the number of finished projects to drop. Instead, the share of projects finished on time rose slightly over six months, and fewer employees left the company. The managers caution, however, that the trial involved only one company and may not apply elsewhere.
c: A company's four-day-week trial went better than expected, though its results may not apply to other companies.
Every company should adopt a four-day workweek.
The company finished fewer projects during the trial.
Employees left the company because of the trial.
w: The managers specifically warn against generalizing.
On-time projects rose slightly.
Fewer employees left.
items.e: The text reports better-than-expected results and the managers' caution that one company's trial may not generalize.

items.p: Some critics dismiss detective novels as formula: a crime, a clever investigator, a solution. Literary scholar Ines Varga argues that this view misses what readers value. The pleasure of the genre, she contends, lies less in the solution than in the investigator's way of noticing, the trained attention that turns an ordinary room into a field of clues, so that readers come away seeing their own surroundings differently.
c: Varga argues that detective novels appeal mainly through the way they model careful observation.
Varga argues that detective novels are superior to other genres.
Critics argue that detective novels have unpredictable solutions.
Varga claims that readers dislike the solutions in detective novels.
w: Varga does not compare genres.
The critics call the genre formulaic, not unpredictable.
She says the solution matters less, not that readers dislike it.
items.e: Varga's central claim is that the genre's pleasure comes from the investigator's way of noticing, which changes how readers see.

items.p: Ecologists long treated dead trees in forests as waste, and some forest managers removed them to reduce fire risk. Recent surveys, however, have found that standing dead trees shelter many nesting birds and that fallen logs hold moisture that seedlings depend on in dry summers. These findings have led some managers to leave a portion of dead wood in place, balancing fire concerns against the habitat it provides.
c: Evidence of dead trees' ecological value has led some managers to stop removing all of them.
Dead trees increase fire risk more than living trees do.
Forest managers should never remove dead trees.
Seedlings grow best in forests with no fallen logs.
w: The text does not compare fire risk from dead and living trees.
Managers now leave a portion in place, balancing fire concerns; the text does not say never remove them.
Fallen logs help seedlings in dry summers.
items.e: The text moves from the old view, to new evidence of habitat value, to managers' changed practice.

items.q: According to the text, why does Mensah argue that the printed scores are only a starting point?
items.p: Music historian Kofi Mensah studied hundreds of handwritten band parts used by a touring brass ensemble in the early 1900s. Pencil markings in the margins, such as cuts, added repeats, and notes like "slower for hall," show that the ensemble altered pieces night to night depending on the venue. Mensah argues that the printed scores therefore record only a starting point, not how the music was actually heard.
c: Markings show that the ensemble changed the music for different performances.
The printed scores were lost before the tour began.
Members of the ensemble could not read music.
The printed scores contained many printing errors.
w: The text does not say the scores were lost.
The members wrote musical markings, so they could read music.
Printing errors are never mentioned.
items.e: The pencil markings show the music was altered for each venue, so the printed scores don't capture what audiences heard.

items.p: Many people assume that bilingual children fall behind in vocabulary. Linguist Hana Sato notes that such children often know fewer words in each individual language than monolingual peers do, but when both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is typically similar or larger. Sato argues that measuring only one language misrepresents what these children know.
c: Sato argues that bilingual children's vocabulary is underestimated when only one language is measured.
Sato argues that bilingual children learn words more slowly than other children.
Bilingual children know more words in each language than monolingual children.
Sato believes vocabulary tests should be eliminated.
w: Sato's point is that their total is similar or larger.
The text says they often know fewer words in each language.
Sato criticizes one way of measuring, not all tests.
items.e: Sato's main claim is that counting one language misrepresents bilingual children's total vocabulary.

items.p: The letter lay unopened on the table for three days. Marcus moved it to make room for his coffee, then for a stack of bills, and once, absurdly, to dust beneath it. He knew the handwriting. He told himself he was simply busy, though the house had never been so clean.
c: Marcus avoids opening a letter while telling himself that he is merely busy.
Marcus does not recognize who sent the letter.
Marcus is too busy with bills to read his mail.
Marcus has lost the letter among his papers.
w: He "knew the handwriting."
The clean house suggests his busyness is an excuse.
He keeps moving the letter, so it is not lost.
items.e: Marcus keeps handling the letter without opening it, and the spotless house shows that "busy" is an excuse.

items.p: City planners often measure a park's value by how many visitors it draws. Urban geographer Leila Haddad suggests a different measure: how long people stay. A plaza that thousands cross on their way elsewhere may be busy, she notes, but a small garden where neighbors linger for an hour may do more to build the everyday familiarity that makes a neighborhood feel safe.
c: Haddad proposes that how long people stay may reflect a park's value better than how many people visit.
Haddad argues that busy plazas should be replaced with small gardens.
Haddad claims that busy plazas make neighborhoods less safe.
City planners usually measure parks by how long visitors stay.
w: She proposes a measure, not replacing plazas.
She says gardens may do more, not that plazas harm safety.
The text says planners usually count visitors.
items.e: Haddad suggests measuring time spent rather than visitor counts, because lingering builds neighborhood familiarity.
